topic: Work Integration for Mechanical Energy Recovery in Chemical Process Systems:State-of-the-Art and Future Directions
title: Work Integration for Mechanical Energy Recovery in Chemical Process Systems:State-of-the-Art and Future Directions
session_title: Plenary: Process Development Division 25th Anniversary Celebratory Session 2 (Invited Talks)
abstract: High‐pressure chemical processes, including Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis, methanol synthesis, Fischer–Tropsch hydrocarbon synthesis, hydrocracking, and hydrotreating, routinely pressurize and subsequently depressurize process streams to meet thermodynamic, kinetic, and separation requirements. Because mechanical energy (electricity) typically costs 4–8 times more per unit than thermal energy (steam), recovering this work through work integration offers substantial economic and environmental benefits. Work integration is achieved by synthesizing work exchanger networks (WENs) that capture and redistribute pressure-derived mechanical energy across the plant. Since the introduction of the concept of WENs in 1996, two principal synthesis methodologies have emerged. The superstructure-based optimization approach centers on compressor–expander trains and embeds all candidate matches into a single MINLP to trade off recovery performance and capital cost. In contrast, the thermodynamic modeling approach employs piston‐type work exchangers, using state‐point analyses to screen high‐value matches before detailed network design. Both methods extend naturally to heat‐integrated WENs, enabling simultaneous recovery of mechanical and thermal energy. In this presentation, we compare the advantages and limitations of each synthesis strategy, review piston‐type exchanger design and dynamic behavior in operation, and explore how emerging tools, such as large language models and digital twins, can accelerate the development of optimal, digitally enabled WENs for next‐generation chemical plants.

topic: Sustainable Process Development for the Real World
title: Sustainable Process Development for the Real World
session_title: Plenary: Process Development Division 25th Anniversary Celebratory Session 2 (Invited Talks)
abstract: Despite decades of innovation in sustainable process development, actual successful implementations and adoption of innovative sustainable processes are limited. This presentation addresses key challenges and misunderstandings contributing to this gap, and offers some potential strategies to improve future success. Key areas of discussion include: Sustainable processes vs green chemistry. (Second law of) thermodynamics. Basic economics and the premium trap. Capital cost estimation and scale-up. Experiments, data, and models. Complexity hides both good and bad ideas. Biology and Reaction and Decarbonization vs. circularity. The development and deployment of commercially-sound sustainable processes is key for the future of the (chemical) process industries, our profession, and ultimately to continued societal development.
